title: "Micronutrient Supplementation for Depressive and Anxiety Symptoms in Adults: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials"
bibliography: vitamins.bib

[]{#sec-title-page}

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

## Objective: {#sec-abstract-objective .unnumbered}
To evaluate the efficacy of micronutrient supplementation for depressive and anxiety symptoms in adults.

## Methods: {#sec-abstract-methods .unnumbered}
MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and PsycINFO were searched from database inception through July 22, 2024, in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials in adults evaluating B vitamins, vitamins C or D, zinc, magnesium, selenium, or iron versus placebo, standard care, or no active supplementation. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 1 tool. Primary outcomes were changes in validated depression or anxiety symptom scores, analyzed as standardized mean differences (SMDs). A Bayesian network meta-analysis estimated effects and 95% credible intervals (CrIs). Of 101 included studies (37,932 participants), 50 low-risk-of-bias studies were included in the primary analysis.

## Results: {#sec-abstract-results .unnumbered}
Vitamin D showed the only credible evidence of benefit versus placebo for depressive symptoms (SMD: -0.32; 95% CrI:-0.51 to -0.13). Selenium also showed a credible estimate (SMD: -0.99; 95% CrI: -1.90 to -0.11), but this finding was based on 2 studies and should be interpreted cautiously. No micronutrient showed credible benefit for anxiety symptoms. Study-level subgroup analyses suggested larger vitamin D effects in trials enrolling participants with baseline deficiency and depressive symptoms.

## Conclusions: {#sec-abstract-conclusions .unnumbered}
Among the micronutrients evaluated, vitamin D had the most consistent evidence of benefit for depressive symptoms. Evidence for anxiety outcomes and for other micronutrients remained limited or inconclusive. Future trials should focus on well-characterized, deficient populations and incorporate biomarker assessment before and after treatment.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Depression and anxiety are among the most prevalent mental health conditions worldwide and remain leading contributors to disability and lost productivity [@stewart_cost_2003; @deady_impact_2022]. These conditions frequently co-occur and often accompany chronic medical illness, further worsening functioning and quality of life [@zhang_global_2026]. Although pharmacologic and psychosocial treatments are effective for many patients, response is often incomplete, relapse is common, and residual symptoms, treatment burden, adverse effects, and barriers to care remain substantial clinical problems [@simon_management_2024; @szuhany_anxiety_2022]. These limitations have sustained interest in adjunctive strategies that are biologically plausible, scalable, and accessible.

Micronutrient supplementation has emerged as one such area of interest. Inadequate intake of several micronutrients relevant to cognitive and psychological health is common worldwide [@passarelli_global_2024], and vitamin and mineral deficiencies are more frequently observed among individuals with depression and anxiety [@sarris_nutritional_2015]. However, the clinical significance of these observations remains uncertain. Micronutrient interventions are often discussed as a broad category despite substantial differences in biological role, baseline nutrient status, dosing, formulation, and study population. The central clinical question is therefore not whether “supplements” are beneficial in general, but whether specific micronutrients improve depressive or anxiety symptoms in adults, and under what conditions.

Micronutrients such as the B vitamins, vitamins D and C, magnesium, zinc, selenium, and iron are involved in biological processes relevant to mood and anxiety regulation [@young_systematic_2019; @bourre_effects_2006]. These nutrients function as prohormones influencing gene expression and as cofactors in enzymatic pathways related to neurotransmitter synthesis, energy metabolism, and neuronal signaling [@young_systematic_2019; @bourre_effects_2006]. They have also been implicated in oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial function, and stress-response pathways that may contribute to depressive and anxiety symptoms [@zielinska_dietary_2023; @wang_zinc_2018; @majewska_mineral_2025; @quan_appropriate_2023]. However, biological plausibility alone is insufficient to guide clinical practice, particularly when trials differ substantially in baseline nutrient status, symptom burden, intervention design, and methodological quality.

Randomized controlled trials have evaluated both single and combined micronutrient interventions for depression and anxiety, but findings have been heterogeneous and difficult to translate clinically [@blampied_broad_2020; @okereke_effect_2020]. Prior systematic reviews have largely focused on individual nutrients or selected populations, limiting the field’s ability to compare evidence across micronutrients and to examine whether baseline nutrient deficiency may modify treatment response [@blampied_broad_2020; @tobin_targeting_2024; @ghaemi_effect_2024; @frost_understanding_2025; @lakhan_nutritional_2010; @boyle_effects_2017; @kamat_therapeutic_2023]. As a result, it remains unclear which micronutrients, if any, have the most credible evidence of benefit for depressive and anxiety symptoms, and whether observed effects are more consistent with nonspecific supplementation or with repletion in biologically relevant subgroups.

In this systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis, we evaluated randomized controlled trials of B vitamins, vitamins C and D, zinc, magnesium, selenium, and iron supplementation for depressive and anxiety symptoms in adults. By synthesizing evidence across these interventions and examining the potential relevance of baseline micronutrient status, we aimed to clarify the comparative evidence for benefit across specific micronutrients and to inform future research and more targeted clinical use.

# Methods

This systematic review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024575661) and followed PRISMA reporting guidelines [@chien_effectiveness_2026].

## Search Strategy {#sec-search}

A comprehensive literature search was conducted from database inception to July 22, 2024, in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines using Ovid MEDLINE, Embase.com, Web of Science Core Collection, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, ClinicalTrials.gov, and APA PsycINFO databases.
The search strategy incorporated controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to anxiety, depression, and supplementation with B vitamins, vitamin C, vitamin D, zinc, magnesium, selenium, or iron. A validated filter was applied to identify randomized controlled trials [@royle_making_2007]. The complete search strategy is provided in the Appendix.

All records were de-duplicated using EndNote [@noauthor_endnote_2023] and imported into Covidence Systematic Review Software [@veritas_health_innovation_covidence_nodate] for screening. Titles, abstracts, and full texts were independently reviewed by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer.

## Eligibility Criteria {#sec-eligibility}

RCTs evaluating the effects of vitamin or mineral supplementation on depressive or anxiety symptoms in adults were included. Non-randomized studies, observational studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, case reports and series, animal studies, and non–peer-reviewed publications were excluded. Given feasibility constraints, RCTs not published in English and articles without accessible full text were also excluded.

Eligible participants included adults ≥18 years old from the general population who exhibited clinically significant depressive or anxiety symptoms or met diagnostic criteria for a depressive or anxiety disorder. Anxiety disorders encompassed social anxiety disorder, panic disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder. Depressive disorders included major depressive disorder, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, persistent depressive disorder, postpartum depression, seasonal affective disorder, dysthymic disorder, and vascular depression. Trials enrolling individuals with bipolar disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, psychotic disorders, schizophrenia, or neurocognitive disorders were excluded.

Eligible interventions included supplementation with B vitamins, vitamin C, vitamin D, zinc, magnesium, selenium, or iron, either alone or in combination. No restrictions were placed on dose, formulation, or duration. Herbal remedies or supplements outside of these prespecified nutrients were excluded. Comparator conditions included placebo, standard care, or no active supplementation.

Eligible trials were required to have a minimum follow-up duration of four weeks, as shorter trials were considered unlikely to capture clinically meaningful changes in depressive or anxiety symptoms. When multiple publications reported on overlapping datasets, the study with the largest sample and most comprehensive outcome data was retained.


## Data Extraction {#sec-data-extraction}
Two reviewers independently extracted data, with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Extracted study characteristics included author, year, country, setting, funding source, recruitment method, randomization procedures, blinding, intervention duration, and assessment timepoints. Participant characteristics included sample size, age, sex distribution, diagnostic criteria, baseline symptom severity, baseline micronutrient status, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and attrition rates. Intervention details included supplement type, dose, formulation, frequency, route of administration, and adherence. Comparator conditions were categorized as placebo, standard care, or no active intervention.

For each study, mean scores and standard deviations for validated depression and anxiety scales at baseline and follow-up were extracted, along with reported changes over time and adverse events. When multiple scales were used within a study, outcomes were preferentially extracted from the most widely validated instrument. When essential data were missing, corresponding authors were contacted for clarification when feasible.

## Risk of Bias Assessment {#sec-risk-bias}

Methodological quality was assessed independently by two reviewers using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 1 (RoB 1) tool for randomized controlled trials, which was the tool available in Covidence at the time of review [@higgins_cochrane_2011; @sterne_rob_2019]. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer consulted when necessary. Studies were evaluated across the seven standard RoB 1 domains and categorized as having low, unclear, or high risk of bias according to criteria in the Cochrane Handbook. Overall risk of bias for each study reflected the highest level of concern across domains. When information was insufficient, investigators were contacted for clarification; if unavailable, the domain was rated as unclear.

## Outcome Measures {#sec-outcomes}

The primary outcome assessed was change in depression or anxiety symptom severity measured with a validated rating scale at the end of the study (e.g., Beck Depression Inventory, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale). Studies that did not report sufficient quantitative outcome data were excluded. Given that different scales were used across trials, outcomes were harmonized using standardized mean differences (SMDs). When multiple scales were reported for the same condition within a study, the most commonly used scale across studies was selected. A complete list of scales and their frequency of use, as well as how outcomes were constructed, is provided in the Appendix. 

Secondary outcomes included pre–post changes in serum micronutrient concentrations and adverse events. For change in serum micronutrients, we expressed differences as mean differences. For adverse events, effect estimates were expressed as odds ratios.

## Statistical Analysis {#sec-stat-analysis}

Analysis was conducted using a Bayesian network meta-analysis that combined direct and indirect comparisons under a hierarchical random-effects model with study-level random effects [@lu_combination_2004]. The primary network meta-analysis was restricted to studies at low overall risk of bias; all other eligible studies—including two low risk of bias studies with interventions comparing doses of the same vitamins—were retained for prespecified sensitivity analyses. Models were fit using the `brms` package in `R`, which implements Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling via `Stan` to estimate posterior distributions of treatment effects [@burkner_advanced_2018; @r_core_team_r_2025; @gabry_cmdstanr_2025]. Additional model details, including priors, number of chains and iterations, convergence diagnostics, and handling of multi-arm trials, are provided in the Appendix.

The assumption of transitivity may be threatened by uneven distributions of baseline vitamin deficiency and baseline depression or anxiety status across interventions. We therefore evaluated transitivity by examining whether key potential effect modifiers were similarly distributed across treatment comparisons. Specifically, we assessed sex distribution, baseline micronutrient deficiency, baseline symptom severity, baseline diagnostic status, and adjunctive antidepressant use, each of which may plausibly influence treatment response. Study- and comparison-level characteristics were visually inspected to identify systematic imbalances across the network. In addition, prespecified network meta-regression models were used to formally evaluate effect modification by these study-level characteristics, and subgroup-specific estimates are reported.

A common between-study heterogeneity parameter (τ) was assumed across interventions within each outcome network. Heterogeneity was interpreted by comparing τ to the scale of observed treatment effects and by examining prediction intervals. Coherence (consistency) was assessed using node-splitting models and a design-by-treatment interaction model [@dias_checking_2010; @dias_evidence_2013]. Residual heterogeneity and inconsistency were further explored using prespecified meta-regression models evaluating potential sources of variability, including risk of bias, baseline symptom severity, baseline micronutrient levels, year and country of study, standard error, and duration of follow-up. Contour-enhanced funnel plots were used to assess potential small-study effects.

When augmentation trials formed a disconnected subnetwork from the main placebo-controlled network, they were modeled separately and did not contribute to indirect comparisons in the primary network.
Certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) framework, which assesses six domains: within-study bias, reporting bias, indirectness, imprecision, heterogeneity, and incoherence [@nikolakopoulou_cinema_2020]. Confidence ratings were generated for all interventions relative to placebo and for all contrasts present in the network (see the Appendix).

```{r}
to_sentence_oxford <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  if (n == 0) return("")
  if (n == 1) return(x)
  if (n == 2) return(paste(x, collapse = " and "))
  paste(paste(x[-n], collapse = ", "), ", and ", x[n], sep = "")
}

vitamin_range_to_text <- function(r) {
  ranges <- c("min", "max")
  txt <- ""
  min <- dose_ranges[[paste0("min_d.", r)]]
  max <- dose_ranges[[paste0("max_d.", r)]]
  
  if (min == max) {
    txt <- glue::glue("the total daily dose was {min}")
    
  } else {
    txt <- glue::glue("the total daily dose ranged from {min} to {max}")
  }
 
  return(txt)
}

vitamin_duration_to_text <- function(r) {
  txt <- ""
  min <- duration %>% filter(grepl(glue::glue("{r}(?![0-9])"), intervention, perl = TRUE)) %>% select(duration) %>% min()
  max <- duration %>% filter(grepl(glue::glue("{r}(?![0-9])"), intervention, perl = TRUE)) %>% select(duration) %>% max()
  
  min_unit <- max_unit <- " weeks"
  if(min == 52) {
    min <- min/52
    min_unit <- " year"
  }
  if(min > 52) {
    min <- min/52
    min_unit <- " years"
  }
  if(max == 52) {
    max <- max/52
    max_unit <- " year"
  }
  if(max > 52) {
    max <- max/52
    max_unit <- " years"
  }
  
  if(min_unit == max_unit) {
    min_unit <- ""
  }
  
  if (min == max) {
    txt <- glue::glue("and the duration of supplementation was {max}{max_unit}")
    
  } else {
    txt <- glue::glue("and the duration of supplementation ranged from {min}{min_unit} to {max}{max_unit}")
  }
 
  return(txt)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: rob info
#| message: false
#| warning: false

qual <- readRDS(here::here("data","quality.rds")) %>% 
    filter(study %in% full_data$study) %>% 
    mutate(study = forcats::fct_recode(study, "Vyas/2023/US" = "Vyas/2023/US/2"))

most_common_bias <- qual %>%
  select(-study, -bias.overall) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "domain",
    values_to = "judgment"
  ) %>%
  filter(judgment != "low") %>%
  group_by(domain, judgment) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(domain) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(domain = forcats::fct_recode(domain %>% as.factor(),
                               "Random sequence generation" = "bias.sequence",
                               "Allocation concealment" = "bias.concealment",
                               "Blinding of participants and personnel" = "bias.blinding.participants",
                               "Blinding of outcome assessment" = "bias.blinding.outcome",
                               "Incomplete outcome data" = "bias.incomplete.outcome",
                               "Selective outcome reporting" = "bias.selective.outcome",
                               "Other sources of bias" = "bias.other"
    )) %>% 
  arrange(desc(n)) %>% 
  slice(1) %>% pull(domain)
```

## Study Selection {#sec-study-selection}

Using the prespecified selection criteria, we identified `r prisma_data$N_initial_studies` records. After removal of `r prisma_data$N_exclude` duplicates, `r prisma_data$N_screened` records underwent title and abstract screening, of which `r prisma_data$N_exclude_screen` were excluded for not meeting eligibility criteria. We then assessed `r prisma_data$N_full_text` full-text articles for eligibility and excluded `r prisma_data$N_exclude_full_text` because of an ineligible intervention, unavailable full text, use of a non-validated measure of depression or anxiety, duplicate data, or inadequate reporting for analysis. The remaining `r prisma_data$N_extracted` studies underwent data extraction and full eligibility review; `r prisma_data$N_exclude_after_extract` were subsequently excluded because they did not meet inclusion criteria or lacked usable quantitative outcome data. This left `r prisma_data$N_included` studies for inclusion in the review. Of these, `r prisma_data$N_main_analysis` low-risk-of-bias studies were included in the primary analysis, and `r prisma_data$N_sensitivity_only` additional eligible studies were retained for sensitivity analyses only. The study selection process is shown in the PRISMA flow diagram (@fig-prisma).

::: {#fig-prisma fig-cap="PRISMA Flow Diagram"}

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="8.5in"}
if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
  knitr::include_graphics("../overall/jpeg/prisma_flow_diagram.jpeg")
} else {
  knitr::include_graphics("../overall/pdf/prisma_flow_diagram.pdf")
}
```
:::

## Characteristics of Included Studies {#sec-results-characteristics}

The `r prisma_data$N_included` included studies were published between `r min(data$year, na.rm = TRUE)` and `r max(data$year, na.rm = TRUE)`. Interventions included B vitamins (`r n_tx_summary$N_B` studies), vitamin C (`r n_tx_summary$N_C`), vitamin D (`r n_tx_summary$N_D`), zinc (`r n_tx_summary$N_zinc`), magnesium (`r n_tx_summary$N_mag`), selenium (`r n_tx_summary$N_selenium`), iron (`r n_tx_summary$N_iron`), and multi-nutrient combinations (`r n_tx_summary$N_multi`). These categories were not mutually exclusive because some studies evaluated combination products containing more than one eligible micronutrient. `r n_tx_summary$N_antidepressant %>% english::Words()` studies evaluated micronutrients as adjuncts to antidepressant treatment. Follow-up ranged from `r min(data$duration, na.rm = TRUE)` weeks to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(data$duration, na.rm = TRUE)/52)` years (median: `r median(data %>% distinct(study, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(duration), na.rm = TRUE)` weeks). Most studies assessed depressive symptoms (n = `r n_depression`; `r round(n_depression/prisma_data$N_included * 100, digits = 1)`%), whereas fewer assessed anxiety symptoms (n = `r n_anxiety`; `r round(n_anxiety/prisma_data$N_included * 100, digits = 1)`%).

Among the `r data %>% filter(bias == "low") %>% distinct(study) %>% nrow()` low-risk-of-bias studies included in the primary analysis, `r n_tx_summary_low$N_B` evaluated B vitamins, `r n_tx_summary_low$N_C` vitamin C, `r n_tx_summary_low$N_D` vitamin D, `r n_tx_summary_low$N_zinc` zinc, `r n_tx_summary_low$N_mag` magnesium, `r n_tx_summary_low$N_selenium` selenium, and `r n_tx_summary_low$N_iron` iron, with `r n_tx_summary_low$N_multi` studies evaluating multi-nutrient combinations. As above, these categories overlapped because some trials included combination interventions. Follow-up ranged from `r min(data %>% filter(bias == "low") %>% pull(duration), na.rm = TRUE)` weeks to `r {mdd <- max(data %>% filter(bias == "low") %>% pull(duration), na.rm = TRUE)/52; if (mdd == as.integer(mdd)) sprintf("%.0f", mdd) else sprintf("%.1f", mdd)}` years (median: `r median(data %>% filter(bias == "low") %>% distinct(study, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(duration), na.rm = TRUE)` weeks). All `r n_depression_low` studies assessed depressive symptoms, and `r n_anxiety_low` (`r round(n_anxiety_low/(data %>% filter(bias == "low") %>% distinct(study) %>% nrow()) * 100)`%) also assessed anxiety symptoms. Additional study characteristics are shown in the Appendix.

## Population Characteristics {#sec-population-characteristics}

Overall, `r sum(data %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(baseline.N)) %>% format(big.mark = ",")` participants were included, with study sample sizes ranging from `r min(data %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(baseline.N), na.rm = TRUE) %>% format(big.mark = ",")` to `r max(data %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(baseline.N), na.rm = TRUE) %>% format(big.mark = ",")`. Of these, `r sum(data %>% filter(bias == "low") %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(baseline.N)) %>% format(big.mark = ",")` were from low risk-of-bias studies. A total of `r sum(data %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(final.N)) %>% format(big.mark = ",")` participants completed follow-up, corresponding to an overall attrition rate of `r sprintf("%.1f", (1 - (sum(data %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(final.N)) / sum(data %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(baseline.N)))) * 100)`%.

Among the studies in the primary analysis, `r sum(data %>% filter(bias == "low") %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(final.N)) %>% format(big.mark = ",")` participants completed follow-up, with study-level completer samples ranging from `r min(data %>% filter(bias == "low") %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(final.N), na.rm = TRUE) %>% format(big.mark = ",")` to `r max(data %>% filter(bias == "low") %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(final.N), na.rm = TRUE) %>% format(big.mark = ",")` and an overall attrition rate of `r sprintf("%.1f", (1 - (sum(data %>% filter(bias == "low") %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(final.N)) / sum(data %>% filter(bias == "low") %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(baseline.N)))) * 100)`%. These studies were more likely to account for missing data, most commonly using last observation carried forward; none used multiple imputation. In these studies, the mean age was `r sprintf("%.2f", weighted.mean(age_low$age, age_low$baseline.N, na.rm = TRUE))` years (range: `r min(age_low$age, na.rm = TRUE)`–`r max(age_low$age, na.rm = TRUE)`), and `r sprintf("%.1f", weighted.mean(male_low$male, male_low$baseline.N, na.rm = TRUE))`% of participants were male.

Across all studies (n = `r prisma_data$N_include`), `r round(nrow(measured %>% filter(total_obs > 0))) %>% as.integer()` (`r round(nrow(measured %>% filter(total_obs > 0))/nrow(measured) * 100)`%) reported at least one baseline micronutrient level. Among low risk-of-bias studies, `r nrow(measured_low %>% filter(total_obs > 0))` (`r round(nrow(measured_low %>% filter(total_obs > 0))/nrow(measured_low) * 100)`%) reported baseline levels; `r nrow(measured_low %>% filter(total_obs == 1))` (`r round(nrow(measured_low %>% filter(total_obs == 1))/nrow(measured_low) * 100)`%) measured one micronutrient and `r nrow(measured_low %>% filter(total_obs >= 2))` measured two.
Among low risk-of-bias studies, weighted mean baseline concentrations were: vitamin B9 `r vit_levels_low %>% summarize(weighted.mean(baseline.B9, baseline.N, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull() %>% vit$numeric_convert_vitamin_from_molar("vitamin B9",.)`, red blood cell B9 `r vit_levels_low %>% summarize(weighted.mean(baseline.rbc.B9, baseline.N, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull() %>% vit$numeric_convert_vitamin_from_molar("rbc.B9",.)`, vitamin B12 `r vit_levels_low %>% summarize(weighted.mean(baseline.B12, baseline.N, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull() %>% vit$numeric_convert_vitamin_from_molar("vitamin B12",.)`, vitamin D `r vit_levels_low %>% summarize(weighted.mean(baseline.D, baseline.N, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull() %>% vit$numeric_convert_vitamin_from_molar("vitamin D",.)`, zinc `r vit_levels_low %>% summarize(weighted.mean(baseline.zinc, baseline.N, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull() %>% vit$numeric_convert_vitamin_from_molar("zinc",.)`, magnesium `r vit_levels_low %>% summarize(weighted.mean(baseline.magnesium, baseline.N, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull() %>% vit$numeric_convert_vitamin_from_molar("magnesium",.)`, selenium `r vit_levels_low %>% summarize(weighted.mean(baseline.selenium, baseline.N, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull() %>% vit$numeric_convert_vitamin_from_molar("selenium",.)`, and ferritin `r vit_levels_low %>% summarize(weighted.mean(baseline.ferritin, baseline.N, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull() %>% vit$numeric_convert_vitamin_from_molar("ferritin",.)`.

Vitamins B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, and C were not measured in low risk-of-bias studies, either because baseline levels were not assessed or because measurements occurred only in studies excluded from the main analysis due to higher risk of bias.

Sex distribution and baseline clinical status varied across comparisons, with some interventions evaluated primarily in female or clinically depressed populations. The distribution of key study-level characteristics across the network is summarized in the Appendix (@sec-trans).

## Intervention Characteristics {#sec-intervention-characteristics}

Vitamin D (`r n_tx_summary_low$N_D` studies) was the most common intervention aside from placebo (`r vitamin_range_to_text('D')`; `r vitamin_duration_to_text('D')`).

B vitamins (`r n_tx_summary_low$N_B` studies) included B1 (`r vitamin_range_to_text('B1')`; `r vitamin_duration_to_text('B1')`), B6 (`r vitamin_range_to_text('B6')`; `r vitamin_duration_to_text('B6')`), B9 (`r vitamin_range_to_text('B9')`; `r vitamin_duration_to_text('B9')`), and B12 (`r vitamin_range_to_text('B12')`; `r vitamin_duration_to_text('B12')`).

Vitamin C (`r n_tx_summary_low$N_C` study) was evaluated at `r vitamin_range_to_text('C')` for `r vitamin_duration_to_text('C')`.

Minerals included zinc (`r n_tx_summary_low$N_zinc`; `r vitamin_range_to_text('zinc')`; `r vitamin_duration_to_text('zinc')`), magnesium (`r n_tx_summary_low$N_mag`; `r vitamin_range_to_text('magnesium')`; `r vitamin_duration_to_text('magnesium')`), selenium (`r n_tx_summary_low$N_selenium`; `r vitamin_range_to_text('selenium')`; `r vitamin_duration_to_text('selenium')`), and iron (`r n_tx_summary_low$N_iron`; `r vitamin_range_to_text('iron')`; `r vitamin_duration_to_text('iron')`). 

`r n_tx_summary_low$N_multi` studies evaluated multi-nutrient combinations, most commonly `r to_sentence_oxford(stringr::str_split(most_common_multi,",") %>% unlist())`.

## Risk of Bias Within Studies {#sec-results-rob}

`r sum("low" == qual$bias.overall)` studies were rated low risk (`r glue::glue("{round(mean('low' == qual$bias.overall) * 100, digits = 2)}%")`), `r sum("some concerns" == qual$bias.overall)` had unclear risk (`r glue::glue("{round(mean('some concerns' == qual$bias.overall) * 100, digits = 2)}%")`), and `r sum("high" == qual$bias.overall)` were high risk of bias (`r glue::glue("{round(mean('high' == qual$bias.overall) * 100, digits = 2)}%")`). The most frequent source of bias was `r most_common_bias %>% stringr::str_to_lower()`. Primary analyses were restricted to low risk-of-bias studies that had usable data. Two low-risk-of-bias studies only had interventions comparing dosing of the same micronutrient and were thus only analyzed in the sensitivity analyses. Domain-level assessments are shown in @fig-rob.

::: {#fig-rob}

![](../overall/pdf/rob.pdf){width=8.5in}

Risk of bias by domain. Studies were assessed by the Risk of Bias 1 tool.
:::

## Effect of Micronutrient Supplementation on Depression Symptoms {#sec-results-depression}

In analyses restricted to studies at low overall risk of bias, only vitamin D and selenium yielded posterior mean estimates with 95% credible intervals excluding the null (@fig-tx).

For vitamin D, the posterior mean effect was `r dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2) %>% as.numeric()` standard deviations compared with placebo (95% CrI, `r dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2) %>% as.numeric()` to `r dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2) %>% as.numeric()`). For context, assuming a standard deviation of approximately 9 points on the Beck Depression Inventory, this corresponds to roughly a 3-point greater improvement relative to placebo; because multiple depression scales were used across studies, this translation is intended as an illustrative approximation.

The posterior mean effect for selenium was larger in magnitude (SMD: `r dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "Selenium") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)`; 95% CrI: `r dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "Selenium") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "Selenium") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`), but this estimate was informed by only `r data %>% filter(intervention == "selenium" & bias == "low" & target == "depression") %>% nrow()` studies (N = `r (data %>% filter(study %in% (data %>% filter(intervention == "selenium" & bias == "low" & target == "depression") %>% pull(study))) %>% distinct(study, intervention, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% pull(baseline.N)) %>% sum()`) and should be regarded as preliminary.

Other micronutrients, including vitamin B6 (SMD: `r dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "B6") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)`, 95% CrI: `r dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "B6") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "B6") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`) and vitamin B1 (SMD: `r dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "B1") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)`, 95% CrI: `r dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "B1") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "B1") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`), showed point estimates suggestive of benefit, but credible intervals were wide and included the null (@fig-tx). CINeMA ratings indicated low confidence for selenium and very low confidence for all other comparisons (see Appendix).

Between-study heterogeneity was substantial: the posterior mean of $\tau$ was `r fit_dep %>% posterior::as_draws_df(variable = "tau")  %>% summary() %>% select(mean) %>% round(digits = 2) %>% as.numeric()` (95% CrI: `r fit_dep %>% posterior::as_draws_df(variable = "tau")  %>% summarize_draws(~quantile(.x, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))) %>% select('2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2) %>% as.numeric()` to `r fit_dep %>% posterior::as_draws_df(variable = "tau")  %>% summarize_draws(~quantile(.x, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))) %>% select('97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2) %>% as.numeric()`), comparable in magnitude to some estimated treatment effects.

Given the uneven distribution of baseline deficiency and depression status across interventions, subgroup and meta-regression analyses were conducted to evaluate potential effect modification. In meta-regression models, baseline deficiency and baseline depression were associated with larger estimated effects of vitamin D. Among populations that were both depressed and vitamin D deficient, the posterior mean effect was `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "yes", depressed == "yes") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)` (95% CrI: `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "yes", depressed == "yes") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "yes", depressed == "yes") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`). In depressed but non-deficient populations, the estimate was similar in magnitude but more uncertain (`r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "no", depressed == "yes") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)`, 95% CrI: `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "no", depressed == "yes") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "no", depressed == "yes") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`). In depressed populations with unknown deficiency status, the posterior mean effect was `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "NA", depressed == "yes") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)` (95% CrI: `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "NA", depressed == "yes") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "NA", depressed == "yes") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`). In non-depressed populations, estimated effects were close to null regardless of deficiency status. CINeMA ratings for vitamin D estimates for depressed populations were rated as low confidence while those in non-depressed populations were rated as very low confidence (see the appendix).

For selenium, subgroup estimates were based on minimal data. In a deficient, non-depressed population (one study), the posterior mean effect was `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "Selenium", def == "yes", depressed == "no") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)` (95% CrI: `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "Selenium", def == "yes", depressed == "no") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "Selenium", def == "yes", depressed == "no") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`). This estimate was rated as moderate confidence following the CINeMA guidelines. In a depressed population with unknown deficiency status (one study), the estimate was `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "Selenium", def == "NA", depressed == "yes") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)` (95% CrI: `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "Selenium", def == "NA", depressed == "yes") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r def_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "Selenium", def == "NA", depressed == "yes") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`). This estimate was rated as very low confidence following CINeMA guidelines. Results for other vitamins are provided in the Appendix.

Dose–response analyses suggested a possible gradient for vitamin D, although credible intervals overlapped across dose categories. For doses <1000 IU/day, the mean difference was `r dose_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", .dose == "<1000 IU") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)` (95% CrI: `r dose_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", .dose == "<1000 IU") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r dose_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", .dose == "<1000 IU") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`), compared with `r dose_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", .dose == "1000-3000 IU") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)` and `r dose_dep_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", .dose == ">3000 IU") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)` at higher dose categories (full estimates in Appendix).
Longer study duration was generally associated with attenuation toward the null, though estimates were imprecise. Vitamin D effects were largest in studies ≤8 weeks and diminished in longer-duration categories (see Sensitivity Analyses for full estimates).

In low risk-of-bias analyses, antidepressant augmentation trials formed a disconnected sub-network and were therefore modeled separately, with antidepressant monotherapy as the reference. These estimates did not contribute to indirect comparisons in the primary network. Augmentation effects were similar in magnitude to antidepressant monotherapy but were based on few studies. For example, only `r data %>% filter(intervention == "antidepressant, D" & target == "depression") %>% nrow()` studies evaluated vitamin D augmentation (SMD: `r ssri_results %>% filter(.trt == "Antidepressant, D") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)`, 95% CrI: `r ssri_results %>% filter(.trt == "Antidepressant, D") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r ssri_results %>% filter(.trt == "Antidepressant, D") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`), while `r data %>% filter(intervention == "antidepressant, B9" & target == "depression" & bias == "low") %>% nrow()` studies examined antidepressants plus vitamin B9 (SMD: `r ssri_results %>% filter(.trt == "Antidepressant, B9") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)`, 95% CrI: `r ssri_results %>% filter(.trt == "Antidepressant, B9") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r ssri_results %>% filter(.trt == "Antidepressant, B9") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`). Similarly, `r data %>% filter(intervention == "antidepressant, B12, B6, B9" & target == "depression" & bias == "low") %>% nrow()` study examined antidepressants plus vitamin B6, B9, and B12 (SMD: `r ssri_results %>% filter(.trt == "Antidepressant, B12, B6, B9") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)`, 95% CrI: `r ssri_results %>% filter(.trt == "Antidepressant, B12, B6, B9") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r ssri_results %>% filter(.trt == "Antidepressant, B12, B6, B9") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`).

## Effect of Micronutrient Supplementation on Anxiety Symptoms {#sec-results-anxiety}

Among studies at low overall risk of bias, no examined vitamins or minerals had 95% credible intervals excluding the null. The largest estimated effect was observed for selenium (SMD `r anx_results %>% filter(.trt == "Selenium") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)`, 95% CrI: `r anx_results %>% filter(.trt == "Selenium") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r anx_results %>% filter(.trt == "Selenium") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`); in contrast to its effect on depression, vitamin D was estimated to have little average effect on anxiety symptoms. Only one low risk-of-bias study evaluated antidepressant augmentation with vitamin D for anxiety, so this estimate is not presented. All estimates were rated as very low confidence according to CINeMA guidelines (see the appendix).

The posterior mean of $\tau$ in the anxiety network was `r fit_anx %>% posterior::as_draws_df(variable = "tau")  %>% summary() %>% select(mean) %>% round(digits = 2) %>% as.numeric()` (95% CrI: `r fit_anx %>% posterior::as_draws_df(variable = "tau")  %>% summarize_draws(~quantile(.x, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))) %>% select('2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2) %>% as.numeric()` to `r fit_anx %>% posterior::as_draws_df(variable = "tau")  %>% summarize_draws(~quantile(.x, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))) %>% select('97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2) %>% as.numeric()`). Despite largely null effects, heterogeneity was substantial.

Subgroup estimates stratified by baseline deficiency and baseline anxiety status likewise yielded no comparisons with credible intervals excluding the null. For vitamin D, the posterior mean effect in deficient populations with baseline anxiety was `r def_anx_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "yes", anxiety == "yes") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)` (95% CrI: `r def_anx_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "yes", anxiety == "yes") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r def_anx_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "yes", anxiety == "yes") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`), and in non-deficient populations with baseline anxiety was `r def_anx_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "no", anxiety == "yes") %>% pull(Estimate) %>% round(digits = 2)` (95% CrI: `r def_anx_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "no", anxiety == "yes") %>% pull('q2.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)` to `r def_anx_results %>% filter(.trt == "D", def == "no", anxiety == "yes") %>% pull('q97.5%') %>% round(digits = 2)`). No studies assessed vitamin D for anxiety in populations with unknown deficiency status. Results for other micronutrients are provided in the Appendix. No clear patterns emerged in duration- or dose-stratified analyses for anxiety outcomes (Appendix).

No clear patterns were observed in duration- or dose-stratified analyses (Appendix).

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

In this systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, vitamin D showed the most consistent evidence of benefit for depressive symptoms among the micronutrients evaluated, particularly in analyses restricted to studies at low-risk-of-bias. By contrast, evidence for anxiety outcomes was inconclusive, and evidence for selenium and other micronutrients was limited by sparse data, imprecision, and substantial heterogeneity. The main implication of these findings is not that micronutrient supplementation is broadly effective for depression and anxiety, but that the current literature is more consistent with a selective and biologically informed interpretation of benefit.

Across low risk-of-bias studies, vitamin D was associated with a modest reduction in depressive symptom severity relative to placebo. That signal is clinically interesting given the broad availability of vitamin D, its generally favorable safety profile when used appropriately, and its biologic relevance to pathways implicated in mood disorders [@sarris_nutritional_2015; @zielinska_dietary_2023; @tobin_targeting_2024]. Vitamin D functions as a neuroactive steroid and has been linked to immune modulation, oxidative stress, neurotrophic signaling, and monoaminergic mechanisms relevant to affective symptoms [@bourre_effects_2006; @wang_zinc_2018; @quan_appropriate_2023]. At the same time, the observed effect should be interpreted with restraint. Between-study heterogeneity was substantial, and the apparent benefit was not uniformly seen across study populations, arguing against a simple conclusion that vitamin D supplementation is effective across all adults with depressive symptoms. The observation that estimated effects were largest in shorter-duration studies (≤8 weeks) and attenuated over longer follow-up may reflect rapid repletion effects that plateau once deficiency is corrected, regression to the mean, or spontaneous remission over time, though the available data do not allow these explanations to be distinguished.

The findings for selenium require even greater caution. Although selenium was associated with a credible reduction in depressive symptoms in the primary analysis, that estimate was derived from a small number of studies with limited sample sizes. Sparse networks can yield unstable estimates, particularly when apparent effects are large. Selenium remains biologically plausible because of its role in antioxidant defense, thyroid hormone metabolism, and inflammatory and neuroendocrine pathways that may intersect with depressive symptoms [@wang_zinc_2018; @majewska_mineral_2025]. However, the current clinical evidence is best viewed as preliminary and hypothesis-generating rather than practice-informing.

For the remaining micronutrients, the absence of statistically credible benefit in low risk-of-bias analyses should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of no effect. For several interventions, including B vitamins, magnesium, zinc, vitamin C, and iron, the available estimates were imprecise, and the credible intervals were wide. This likely reflects a combination of sparse evidence, heterogeneity in dose and formulation, differences in baseline nutrient status and symptom severity, variation in trial duration, and inconsistent outcome measurement [@young_systematic_2019; @zielinska_dietary_2023; @tobin_targeting_2024]. In nutritional psychiatry, pooled null findings may therefore obscure meaningful effects in narrower biologic or clinical subgroups, just as positive findings may be diluted when deficient and replete participants are analyzed together.

 A key contribution of this review is to emphasize baseline micronutrient status, particularly deficiency in relation to depression and anxiety outcomes. Fewer than half of low-risk-of-bias studies (24 of 50; 48%) included participants with deficient pre-intervention levels, defined using established micronutrient-specific thresholds (e.g., vitamin D <20 ng/mL, selenium <70 µg/L, vitamin B6 <20 nmol/L, vitamin B1 <70 nmol/L). Although 24 studies enrolled deficient populations, only sixteen examined the full pathway linking baseline deficiency, supplementation, and depression outcomes. This limits clinical interpretability. Trials that enroll heterogeneous populations containing both deficient and replete individuals may underestimate the effect of repletion by averaging across participants with materially different biologic starting points [@young_systematic_2019; @tobin_targeting_2024]. The present findings are therefore more consistent with a deficiency-informed framework than with a universal supplementation model. In that framework, micronutrients are not understood as nonspecific treatments for all depressive or anxiety symptoms, but as potentially relevant interventions in subgroups with biologically meaningful deficiency.

This interpretation was most clearly supported for vitamin D. Secondary analyses suggested that baseline deficiency and baseline depression status were associated with larger estimated effects of vitamin D, but these findings should be interpreted cautiously because they reflect study-level rather than patient-level effect modification and are therefore more vulnerable to bias and overinterpretation [@zielinska_dietary_2023; @tobin_targeting_2024; @schandelmaier_development_2020]. Vitamin D was also the only nutrient for which the evidence base was sufficiently developed to support this degree of subgroup exploration, which limits broader conclusions about other micronutrients. Even so, these results strengthen the rationale for future trials that stratify or enrich enrollment according to baseline nutrient status rather than assuming homogeneous treatment effects across clinically diverse populations.

The clinical implications of these findings are accordingly narrower than broad enthusiasm for “supplements” might suggest. The present evidence does not support indiscriminate micronutrient supplementation for depression or anxiety. Rather, it supports a cautious and evidence-based approach in which targeted assessment and correction of deficiency may have a role in selected patients. Although micronutrients are often perceived as inherently benign, that assumption should not substitute for clinical judgment. Dose-related toxicity, variable efficacy, and potential interactions remain relevant considerations, particularly when supplementation is used outside documented or suspected deficiency states [@wang_zinc_2018; @biesalski_multivitaminmineral_2017].

This review has several strengths. It used a comprehensive search strategy, duplicate screening and data extraction, explicit risk-of-bias assessment, and a primary analytic approach restricted to low-risk-of-bias trials. It also evaluated a prespecified range of vitamins and minerals while excluding broader nutraceutical, herbal, and dietary interventions, allowing a more focused assessment of micronutrient supplementation as a clinically interpretable category. Several limitations should also be emphasized. Included trials varied substantially in participant selection, intervention characteristics, and outcome measures, contributing to heterogeneity. Baseline biomarker assessment was inconsistently reported, limiting mechanistic interpretation and constraining subgroup analyses. Evidence for several nutrients remained sparse and vulnerable to small-study effects. Multi-nutrient formulations were difficult to interpret because of heterogeneity in composition and dosing. Confidence was low or very low for many comparisons. As with any evidence synthesis, our conclusions are constrained by the quality and completeness of the underlying literature.

Future trials should address these limitations directly. Studies should preferentially stratify or enrich enrollment based on baseline nutrient status, measure biochemical correction alongside psychiatric outcomes, and evaluate micronutrients within clearly defined treatment contexts, including adjunctive use where appropriate. Greater consistency in outcome reporting, better characterization of dose and duration, and more systematic safety assessment will be necessary to move this literature from biologic plausibility to clinically actionable evidence [@young_systematic_2019; @tobin_targeting_2024; @biesalski_multivitaminmineral_2017].

In conclusion, vitamin D had the most consistent evidence of benefit for depressive symptoms among the micronutrients evaluated, whereas evidence for anxiety outcomes remained inconclusive and evidence for other micronutrients was limited or uncertain. These findings are more consistent with a targeted, deficiency-informed framework for future research and clinical use than with universal supplementation. Further trials should focus on well-characterized populations, incorporate biomarker assessment before and after intervention, and determine whether biochemical repletion corresponds to meaningful psychiatric improvement.
